Knowledge center/How I work

Documentation

The documents every neon1 project keeps, what each one is for, and how they stay true: READMEs, changelogs, decision records, and runbooks.

Type
Standard
Edition
1.0
Updated
November 9, 2026
For
Developers
Download PDF

Documentation lets someone use, run, or change a project without asking its author. It's written once, in one place, kept next to the code it describes, and updated in the same change as the code.

Every project has

FileForContains
README.mdAnyone arriving at the projectWhat it is, who it's for, its status, how to run, test, and deploy it, and its license
CHANGELOG.mdPeople using itWhat changed in each release, newest first. See versioning
LICENSEAnyone reusing itThe license text, plus NOTICE when required
SECURITY.mdAnyone who finds a problemHow to report it privately. See the security disclosure policy

Larger projects add:

FileForContains
VCS-ETIQUETTE.md or CONTRIBUTING.mdContributorsAny rules stricter than the version control standard
Decision recordsFuture maintainersWhy a significant choice was made, the options considered, and what would change it
RunbooksWhoever operates itStep-by-step tasks such as deploy, roll back, restore, and rotate a secret

Write by purpose

Following Diátaxis, each document does one of four jobs, and doesn't mix them:

  • Tutorial: learning by doing, for a newcomer.
  • How-to: steps to finish a specific task.
  • Reference: exact facts to look up, such as commands, settings, and fields.
  • Explanation: why things are the way they are.

A README usually holds a short version of each and links out when one grows.

Decision records

Write one when a choice is costly to reverse: a database, a framework, a hosting model, a license. Keep it to a page: the context, the decision, the options rejected and why, and what would make us revisit it. Number them and never delete one. A changed decision gets a new record that replaces the old one. The tool and architecture decision form is a template.

Runbooks

Prerequisites come first, then commands in the order they're run, each with what you should see and what to do if you don't. Commands are copied exactly and tested. A runbook nobody has followed is a draft.

Keeping docs true

  • Docs change in the same commit as the behavior they describe.
  • A checked fact beats a remembered one. Commands in a README should be run before a release.
  • One source for each fact. Link to it instead of copying it, so it can't drift. That's why neon1's public words live once, in neon1-corpus.
